artiest/ginger-rogers.text:
Ginger Rogers was born Virginia Katherine McMath on 16 July 1911 in Independence, Missouri, and grew up in Kansas City and Fort Worth. She got her nickname from a young cousin who could not pronounce Virginia. In 1925, aged fourteen, she won a Charleston contest, after which she spent months touring with a vaudeville act. She then became a Broadway actress. In George and Ira Gershwin's Girl Crazy she became a star at the age of nineteen. Fred Astaire helped the dancers with the choreography at the time.

In the 1930s she made nine films with Astaire for RKO, including The Gay Divorcee in 1934, Top Hat in 1935 and Swing Time in 1936. These films are regarded as groundbreaking for the film musical genre and brought RKO some of its greatest successes. She then turned to drama and comedy. For Kitty Foyle (1940) she won an Oscar for Best Actress. In 1949 she appeared opposite Astaire once more in The Barkleys of Broadway. In all, she made 73 films.

Rogers was an actress, dancer and singer. Thanks to her pairing with Astaire, dance in film became a form of storytelling that said as much as the words did. Her name appears on many albums of songs from those films, at a time when film music set the tone for popular music.
artiest/ginger-rogers.listen: Listen to a song from Top Hat as sung and danced by Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire. Notice how light and easy the singing sounds, as if conversation simply slips into music.

artiest/gioachino-rossini.text: Within a few years Gioachino Rossini became the most famous opera composer in Europe, and he wrote almost forty operas. His music teems with rapid vocal ornamentation and with long crescendos in which the orchestra grows steadily louder and fuller. According to tradition, he wrote Il barbiere di Siviglia (1816) in a matter of weeks. After Guillaume Tell in 1829 he lived for almost forty more years, mostly in Paris, without writing another opera.
artiest/gioachino-rossini.listen: Listen to Largo al factotum and hear how Figaro lists his own name and talents faster and faster, like an early rapper.

artiest/giorgio-gaslini.text:
Giorgio Gaslini was an Italian jazz pianist, composer and conductor. He was born on 22 October 1929 and died on 29 July 2014 in Borgo Val di Taro, near Parma. He began performing at the age of thirteen and recorded with his jazz trio at sixteen. In the 1950s and 1960s he played with a quartet of his own. He was the first Italian musician to be named as a new talent in the Down Beat poll, and the first Italian to be officially invited to a jazz festival in the United States, in New Orleans in 1976 and 1977.

He worked with important American soloists, among them Anthony Braxton. His albums include Oltre (1963), Un Amore (1965), Segnali (1968) and Ballate e canzoni (1970). He was the first to teach jazz at the Santa Cecilia Academy in Rome, in 1972 and 1973. From 1991 to 1995 he wrote works for Carlo Actis Dato's Italian Instabile Orchestra.

Outside jazz, Gaslini wrote symphonic works, operas and ballets, which were performed at La Scala in Milan and in other Italian theatres, and he composed film music. In this way he was a bridge between the Italian classical tradition and modern jazz, and he showed that jazz could have a voice of its own in Europe too.
artiest/giorgio-gaslini.listen: Listen to a piece from the album Oltre and notice how the piano plays melodically on the one hand and lets free, sharp chords ring out on the other. It is a good introduction to his style.

artiest/giorgio-moroder.text: Giorgio Moroder comes from South Tyrol and worked as a producer in Munich from the late 1960s. With Donna Summer he made I Feel Love (1977), a disco hit created almost entirely with synthesizers and a sequencer. He brought that technique to film. For Alan Parker's Midnight Express (1978) he wrote pulsating electronic music, for which he won an Oscar. American Gigolo (1980), Cat People (1982), with a title song sung by David Bowie, and Scarface (1983) followed. Moroder also won Oscars for the songs Flashdance... What a Feeling (1983) and Take My Breath Away from Top Gun (1986).
artiest/giorgio-moroder.listen: Notice the continuous sequencer pulse in the bass, and how the music is built up like a disco track.

artiest/giorgis-koutsourelis.text:
Giorgis Koutsourelis was a Greek composer, born in 1914 in Kissamos on Crete. He died in the same place in June 1994. His name is linked above all to a single melody: Armenohorianos Syrtos. A syrtos is a traditional Greek folk dance, and the theme of this piece became the starting point for the song that Mikis Theodorakis wrote and that most people know as Zorba's dance.

In this way a line runs from a Cretan dance melody to one of the best-known Greek sounds in the world. Theodorakis's song belongs to the film Zorba the Greek and has been many listeners' introduction to Greek music. Anyone who wants to hear where the melody came from has to go back to the work of Koutsourelis. It shows how a folk melody from a small town on Crete travelled the world in another form. There is a compilation album of authentic recordings from the years 1935 to 1955, released in 1994, which lets you hear what Greek music sounded like in his day.
artiest/giorgis-koutsourelis.listen: First listen to Zorba's dance by Mikis Theodorakis and notice how the melody keeps getting faster. Then search for a recording of a syrtos and hear which dance melody lies behind it.

artiest/giorgos-batis.text:
Giorgos Batis, born Giorgos Tsoros, was one of the first rebetes to influence rebetiko, the urban Greek music that had its roots in the port districts. He was born in 1885 in Methana and moved as a child to Piraeus, the port city near Athens. From 1912 to 1918 he served in the Greek army. In the mid-1920s he opened a music school called Carmen.

In 1931 he opened a café called Georges Baté. It became one of the most important venues for rebetiko. The café attracted musicians who met there and developed the new style further. Besides his work as a musician, he sold home-made remedies for toothache and other minor ailments as a quack. He owned a large collection of instruments.

Batis died on 10 March 1967 in Piraeus. He never became a famous singer or composer, but his name stands for the first generation that gave rebetiko its place. Anyone who wants to understand later Greek music will find the beginning of that history in him and his café.
artiest/giorgos-batis.listen: Listen to an old rebetiko recording and notice the bouzouki, a stringed instrument with a sharp, metallic sound. Hear how raw and direct the voice sounds.

artiest/giovanni-battista-pergolesi.text:
Giovanni Battista Pergolesi was born on 4 January 1710 in Jesi as Giovanni Battista Draghi. The name Pergolesi refers to Pergola, the town his ancestors came from. He was taught in Jesi and in 1725 went to Naples to study further. He was a composer, violinist and organist, and was regarded as one of the finest Italian musicians of the first half of the eighteenth century. He died of tuberculosis at the age of twenty-six, on 16 or 17 March 1736 in Pozzuoli.

His best-known opera is La serva padrona (1733), a comic intermezzo that became popular in its own right. When it was performed in Paris in 1752, it set off the Querelle des Bouffons, a fierce debate about French and Italian opera. He also wrote serious operas, such as L'Olimpiade in 1735, and church music. His Stabat Mater of 1736, for soprano, alto, strings and basso continuo, is his best-known sacred work.

After his death his fame grew enormously. More than three hundred works were attributed to him, of which modern scholars regard only about thirty as genuine. Stravinsky's ballet Pulcinella (1920) is also a tribute to his style, although many of its pieces turn out to be by other composers. His music can be found on many albums of Baroque music.
artiest/giovanni-battista-pergolesi.listen: Listen to the opening of the Stabat Mater and notice how the two vocal parts follow each other and move together. Hear how the strings support them softly.

artiest/giovanni-gabrieli.text: Giovanni Gabrieli was organist and composer at St Mark's in Venice, a church with galleries facing each other. He wrote for groups of singers and wind players who answered one another from different places, and he was one of the first to notate precisely which instrument plays which part. In his Sonata pian e forte (1597) he also indicates when to play softly and when loudly. His pupil Heinrich Schütz took that style to Germany.
artiest/giovanni-gabrieli.listen: Listen to the Sonata pian e forte and hear how the soft, dark group of wind instruments is suddenly answered by the full, loud tutti.

artiest/giovanni-pierluigi-da-palestrina.text: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina was a choirmaster in Rome, at St Peter's among other places, and wrote more than a hundred masses. After the Council of Trent the Church wanted the sung text to remain intelligible, and Palestrina became the model of a clear, balanced polyphony. According to a later legend, his Missa Papae Marcelli thereby saved polyphonic church music. His style was taught for centuries as the model of pure counterpoint.
artiest/giovanni-pierluigi-da-palestrina.listen: Listen to the Kyrie and hear how smoothly the voices move in small steps, without grating dissonances or large leaps.

artiest/girls-generation.text:
Girls' Generation, called Sonyeo Sidae in Korea and also known as SNSD, is a South Korean girl group formed by SM Entertainment. The name means Generation of Girls. The group has eight members: Taeyeon, Sunny, Tiffany, Hyoyeon, Yuri, Sooyoung, Yoona and Seohyun. Originally there were nine, until Jessica left. Girls' Generation debuted on 5 August 2007 with the single Into the New World from the Korean album of the same name.

In 2009 the group broke through with Gee, which stood at number one on KBS's Music Bank for nine weeks in a row, a record, and was the most popular song of the 2000s on Melon. In 2011 the group entered the Japanese market with a Japanese album of the same name, which, according to the RIAJ, became the first album by a non-Japanese girl group to sell a million copies. The third Korean album, The Boys (2011), was the best-selling album in South Korea that year. Other releases include Oh! in 2010, I GOT A BOY in 2013 and Holiday Night in 2017.

The group's characteristic styles are electropop and bubblegum pop, but the sound varied widely, taking in hip hop, R&B and EDM. In 2017 Billboard named them the Top K-pop Girl Group of the Past Decade. Girls' Generation belongs to the wave that made K-pop known outside Asia, with smooth production, sharply choreographed dance and several singers who each have a role of their own.
artiest/girls-generation.listen: Listen to Gee and notice the short, constantly repeated phrases and the playful, electronic sound. Who sings which part, and how do the voices take turns?

artiest/giuseppe-becce.text: Giuseppe Becce was born in 1877 in Lonigo, near Vicenza, and settled in Berlin. In 1913 he played the title role in the film Richard Wagner and also wrote the music for it. His most important contribution was the Kinothek, which appeared from 1919: a library of short pieces of music, arranged by mood and situation, such as suspense, love or pursuit. Cinema musicians could quickly put together an accompaniment from it. In 1927 he published a large handbook on film music with Hans Erdmann and Ludwig Brav. Becce also wrote scores of his own, including for Murnau's Der letzte Mann (1924). That music has survived only in part; for the restoration of 2003 the composer Detlev Glanert completed it and orchestrated it.
artiest/giuseppe-becce.listen: Notice how short, characteristic pieces are placed one after another: each piece belongs to a single mood and changes as soon as the scene changes.

artiest/giuseppe-patane.text:
Giuseppe Patanè was an Italian opera conductor. He was born on 1 January 1932 in Naples, the son of the conductor Franco Patanè, and studied in his native city. He made his debut there in 1951. In 1961 and 1962 he was principal conductor of the opera in Linz. From 1985 to 1989 he was chief conductor of the Münchner Rundfunkorchester.

His name appears on many opera recordings. These include I Capuleti e i Montecchi (1976), Madama Butterfly (1985), Carmen and Gianni Schicchi (1988), Cavalleria rusticana, Pagliacci and Suor Angelica (1988), and Il barbiere di Siviglia (1989). That repertoire runs from Rossini and Bellini to Puccini, Bizet and Mascagni. He accompanied many well-known singers, and the recordings let you hear how a conductor carries their voices.

Patanè died of a heart attack on 29 May 1989 while conducting Il barbiere di Siviglia at the Bavarian State Opera in Munich. He was taken to hospital, where he died. He left two daughters. His work shows how important the conductor is to the sound of a recording history that is known mainly for its singers.
artiest/giuseppe-patane.listen: Listen to a recording of Madama Butterfly conducted by Patanè and notice how the orchestra follows the singers in the soft and the loud passages. Hear how the conductor lets the tempo breathe.

artiest/giuseppe-verdi.text: Giuseppe Verdi came from a village near Busseto and made his breakthrough in 1842 at La Scala in Milan with Nabucco, whose chorus of the slaves, Va, pensiero, later became a symbol of Italian unification. He always sought out the strongest dramatic situation and wrote melodies that stick in the mind at once. In Rigoletto (1851) the Duke sings the carefree La donna è mobile while the audience already knows how badly it will end. His operas are still at the core of the repertoire.
artiest/giuseppe-verdi.listen: Listen to La donna è mobile and hear how the orchestra plays the tune in advance, so simple that you can sing along after hearing it once.

artiest/gladys-knight-en-the-pips.text:
Gladys Knight & the Pips was a family group from Atlanta, Georgia. In 1952 the eight-year-old Gladys Knight won a talent contest on television. That same year she sang at her brother Merald's birthday party, together with him, her sister Brenda and their cousins William and Eleanor Guest. They called themselves The Pips, after the nickname of a cousin. The group won talent contests in Atlanta and got to open for Jackie Wilson and Sam Cooke. In 1961 came their first hit, Every Beat of My Heart, and from that year the group was called Gladys Knight & the Pips.

In 1966 they signed with Motown. There, in 1967, they recorded I Heard It Through the Grapevine, the first version of that song to become a hit, although Marvin Gaye's version a year later was bigger still. At Motown they went on to record If I Were Your Woman and Neither One of Us, which won a Grammy. Even so, Gladys Knight felt she was treated as second-rate there. In 1973 the group moved to Buddah Records, where their most successful period began with Midnight Train to Georgia, their only number one hit, and I've Got to Use My Imagination.

In the group Gladys Knight's voice came first, with the Pips as backing singers. On stage they stood out for their polished shows, with fast dance steps devised for the Pips by the choreographer Cholly Atkins. In 1989 the Pips called it a day and Gladys Knight continued as a solo artist. The group was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/gladys-knight-en-the-pips.listen: Listen to I Heard It Through the Grapevine by Gladys Knight & the Pips and compare it with Marvin Gaye's version. Notice the faster tempo and how the Pips answer Gladys Knight's lead vocal.

artiest/glen-matlock.text:
Glen Matlock is an English bass player, born on 27 August 1956 in Kensal Green in London. He attended Saint Martin's School of Art and worked in Sex, Malcolm McLaren's clothes shop. There he met the guitarist Steve Jones and the drummer Paul Cook. Together they formed the first line-up of the Sex Pistols. Matlock played bass and sang backing vocals on Anarchy in the UK. He is credited as a writer on ten of the twelve tracks on Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols, even though he had already left the band by then.

In February 1977 he left the group. McLaren said at the time that he had been thrown out because he liked the Beatles. Matlock himself said that he was fed up with the hassle, and that there was tension with Johnny Rotten. His place was taken by Sid Vicious. He then formed Rich Kids, a new wave and power pop band with Midge Ure and Rusty Egan, who had a hit in England in 1978 with Rich Kids. He also played on albums by Iggy Pop and The Damned.

Matlock later rejoined the Sex Pistols for reunion tours in 1996, 2002, 2003, 2007 and 2008. He also played with the Faces and made records of his own, such as Who's He Think He Is When He's at Home? (1996). He is the melodic writer behind the first punk hits.
artiest/glen-matlock.listen: Listen to Anarchy in the UK and notice the bass guitar, which plays a steady, fast line beneath the sharp guitars. Hear how the bass drives the song forward.

artiest/glenn-gould.text:
Glenn Gould was a Canadian pianist and radio producer, born on 25 September 1932 in Toronto and died on 4 October 1982. His mother gave him piano lessons, and at the age of ten he entered the Toronto conservatory. At twelve he passed his final piano examination with the highest marks. In 1952, together with his childhood friend Robert Fulford, he founded New Music Associates, which organised his first performances, including his debut with Bach's Goldberg Variations.

With The Goldberg Variations of 1956 he became world famous. He was regarded as one of the greatest pianists of the twentieth century, above all as an interpreter of Bach. His playing stood out for its technical mastery and its ability to make Bach's polyphony audible with clarity. He sat low at the piano and played at a fast tempo, yet every note remained separate and distinct. He left most Romantic piano music alone. He chose mainly Bach and Beethoven, and also Berg, Schoenberg and Křenek, among others.

Gould was also a writer and broadcaster. He made television programmes about classical music and three radio documentaries, the Solitude Trilogy, about remote parts of Canada, in which he edited voices and sounds together as music. In this way he showed that a recording can itself be an art form.
artiest/glenn-gould.listen: Listen to the opening of the Goldberg Variations of 1956 and notice how each hand plays a melody of its own. Hear how clearly you can follow both lines at once.

artiest/glenn-miller.text: The trombonist and arranger Glenn Miller worked in the 1920s and 1930s in the orchestras of Ben Pollack and the Dorsey Brothers, among others. In 1938 he started a big band of his own with a recognisable sound: a clarinet playing the melody above four saxophones. Between 1939 and 1942 he had a string of enormous hits, such as Moonlight Serenade, In the Mood and Chattanooga Choo Choo, the first record to sell a million copies. In 1942 he joined the army and led an orchestra that entertained the Allied troops. In December 1944 his plane disappeared over the Channel. His music became a symbol of the war years and the Liberation.
artiest/glenn-miller.listen: Listen to the sound of the clarinet on top of the saxophone section.

artiest/glenn-miller-and-his-orchestra.text:
Glenn Miller and His Orchestra was an American swing band founded by the trombonist Glenn Miller in 1938. Miller had played as an accompanist in New York in the 1920s and then turned to arranging, including for Artie Shaw and Benny Goodman. He studied with the theorist Joseph Schillinger. A first orchestra from 1937 did not last long. His second, formed in March 1938, had its breakthrough when in 1939 it was given the summer residency at the Glen Island Casino near New York, with radio broadcasts across the whole country.

The characteristic sound came from a clarinet and a tenor saxophone playing the melody together, with three other saxophones providing the harmony. In April 1939 the orchestra recorded Moonlight Serenade, which became the band's signature tune. In August came In the Mood, with its opening riff and the duelling saxophones of Tex Beneke and Al Klink. In 1940 came Tuxedo Junction and Pennsylvania 6-5000.

The orchestra became the most popular and commercially successful dance orchestra of the swing era. It had sixteen number one singles and sixty-nine top ten hits. It continued until 1942, when Miller joined the US Army Air Forces. He disappeared over the Channel in December 1944. His arrangements continue to shape our picture of the big band.
artiest/glenn-miller-and-his-orchestra.listen: Listen to In the Mood and notice how the saxophones and trumpets alternate. Hear the duel between the two tenor saxophones halfway through.

artiest/glenn-miller-orchestra.text:
The Glenn Miller Orchestra is an American big band that has kept Glenn Miller's music alive since 1956. It is a new incarnation of the famous orchestras of the 1930s and 1940s. The original orchestra played from 1937 to 1942, when Miller joined the Air Force and led an orchestra of his own there. On 15 December 1944 he disappeared over the Channel and was never found.

In 1946 Miller's widow gave permission for a new band under the name Glenn Miller Orchestra, led by the saxophonist and singer Tex Beneke. Many members of the Air Force orchestra played in it. Beneke did not want to follow the old arrangements exactly, and that clashed with Miller's heirs, who wanted an orchestra that would be associated above all with Miller.

The second relaunch came in 1956, after the success of the film The Glenn Miller Story. Miller's widow asked Ray McKinley, who had led the Air Force orchestra, to lead a new orchestra. He stayed until 1966. He was followed by, among others, Buddy DeFranco, Larry O'Brien, Gary Tole and Nick Hilscher, and since 2021 Erik Stabnau. In England, Europe and Scandinavia, too, groups play under the name with permission. In this way the sounds of the swing years can still be heard live.
artiest/glenn-miller-orchestra.listen: Listen to the album In the Digital Mood (1983) and pay attention to the recording. Hear how the orchestra uses modern technology to imitate the classic Miller sound of clarinet and saxophones.

artiest/glenn-slater.text:
Glenn Slater is an American lyricist for musicals, born on 28 January 1968 in Brooklyn and raised in East Brunswick, New Jersey. He became interested in theatre at high school, after failing as a songwriter in a band. In 1990 he graduated from Harvard. He wrote lyrics for the revue Newyorkers in 2001 and for six editions of the Ringling Brothers and Barnum and Bailey circus.

His first work with the composer Alan Menken was the film Home on the Range in 2004 and the musical Sister Act. For the stage version of The Little Mermaid (2008) he wrote the new lyrics; the film's original lyricist, Howard Ashman, had died in 1991. With Andrew Lloyd Webber he made Love Never Dies, the sequel to The Phantom of the Opera, which premiered in the West End in 2010. He also wrote the songs for Disney's Tangled and for Galavant. In 2015 he worked with Lloyd Webber again on School of Rock.

He was nominated three times for a Tony Award, for The Little Mermaid, Sister Act and School of Rock. For I See the Light from Tangled he received a Grammy and an Oscar nomination in 2012. Slater makes sure that the songs in a musical move the story forward, including those of School of Rock.
artiest/glenn-slater.listen: Listen to I See the Light from Tangled and notice how the lyrics turn a small encounter into a big feeling. Hear how the singers complement each other in the chorus.

artiest/globe-unity-orchestra.text:
The Globe Unity Orchestra is a free jazz ensemble from Germany. It came into being in the autumn of 1966, when the pianist Alexander von Schlippenbach was commissioned by the Berlin Jazz Festival to put together a large orchestra. It made its debut on 3 November at the Berliner Philharmonie. There it combined the quartet of Gunter Hampel, the quintet of Manfred Schoof and the trio of Peter Brötzmann.

In the years that followed, other European and American musicians joined, among them Anthony Braxton, Steve Lacy, Evan Parker, Albert Mangelsdorff, Willem Breuker and the drummers Paul Lovens and Paul Lytton. The orchestra was described as one of the most remarkable gatherings of avant-garde jazz since the AACM big bands. In the late 1970s it also played in New Delhi, at the Jazz Yatra. Its records include Globe Unity, Jahrmarkt, Compositions and Intergalactic Blow. The last concert of its most important period took place in 1987 at the Chicago Jazz Festival. For the fortieth anniversary in 2006 a new line-up came together, with Kenny Wheeler, Paul Rutherford and George E. Lewis, among others.

The orchestra showed that free jazz was not meant only for small groups but could also work in a large ensemble, and it gave European improvised music a face of its own.
artiest/globe-unity-orchestra.listen: Listen to the album Globe Unity (1967) and notice how the wind instruments play at the same time without a fixed melody. Hear how the chaos still becomes a whole.

artiest/gloria-jones.text:
Gloria Jones is an American singer and songwriter, born in 1945 in Cincinnati, Ohio. At the age of seven she moved to Los Angeles, where she began to sing. As a schoolgirl she formed the gospel group The COGIC Singers with Billy Preston, among others. The Los Angeles pop scene then drew her in. In 1964 the songwriter Ed Cobb discovered her, and with his Heartbeat she had her first hit.

In the mid-1960s she recorded another of Cobb's songs: Tainted Love. In America it went largely unnoticed, but in the north of England it became a favourite in the northern soul clubs, where young people danced all night to fast American soul records. There Jones was nicknamed the Queen of Northern Soul. She later wrote for Motown, including If I Were Your Woman for Gladys Knight & the Pips. She also appeared in the musical Hair, and she had a classical piano training behind her.

From 1973 to 1977 Jones sang and played clavinet in T. Rex, Marc Bolan's glam rock band. The two began a relationship and in 1975 had a son. Bolan produced her album Vixen (1976). Tainted Love got a second life in 1981, when Soft Cell made a synth-pop version of it that became a worldwide hit. In this way the song shows how a forgotten soul record grew, by way of the British dance floor, into a classic.
artiest/gloria-jones.listen: Listen to Tainted Love by Gloria Jones and notice the fast, danceable soul rhythm and her powerful voice. Then compare it with the Soft Cell version: what stays the same and what changes?

artiest/goblin.text: Goblin was a progressive rock band from Rome centred on the keyboard player Claudio Simonetti. For Dario Argento's giallo Profondo rosso (1975) they first played music by Giorgio Gaslini. When Gaslini left after a quarrel, Argento let the band write the score itself. The main theme, with a repeated organ and bass motif, became a hit in Italy. For Suspiria (1977) they went further: Moog synthesizer, celesta, bouzouki, tabla, whispering and screaming create a hypnotic, frightening sound. They then wrote the music for the European version of George Romero's Dawn of the Dead (1978). Goblin brought the sound of rock and synthesizer to the horror film. That work influenced a great deal of later synthesizer horror.
artiest/goblin.listen: Notice the short, constantly repeated motif in keyboards and bass, and the voices and effects that take part like instruments.

artiest/goffredo-petrassi.text:
Goffredo Petrassi was an Italian composer, conductor and teacher, born on 16 July 1904 in Zagarolo near Rome and died on 3 March 2003. At fifteen he began working in a music shop to help his family, and there he became fascinated by music. In 1928 he entered the Santa Cecilia conservatory in Rome, where he studied organ and composition for five years with Vincenzo di Donato. Later he learned fugue and composition with Alessandro Bustini.

His early work was part of an effort by Italian composers to bring about a national revival of classical music. It was neoclassical in style, influenced by Bartók, Hindemith and Stravinsky. His works from that time include the Partita for orchestra (1932), the Concerto for orchestra (1934), the Piano Concerto (1936 to 1939) and Magnificat. Later he experimented with influences from after Webern and with texts of widely differing kinds, from Latin hymns to Ariosto's La follia d'Orlando and Ritratto di Don Chisciotte, which is based on the figure created by Cervantes. In 1986 he stopped composing because his eyesight was failing.

From 1940 to 1960 he was professor of composition at the Santa Cecilia conservatory, and then until 1978 he gave masterclasses at the Accademia di Santa Cecilia. He was also artistic director of La Fenice and a teacher at the Mozarteum in Salzburg. He is regarded as one of the most influential Italian composers of the twentieth century.
artiest/goffredo-petrassi.listen: Listen to his Concerto for orchestra and notice how the orchestra plays as a whole made up of separate groups. Hear how tight and clear the rhythms sound.

artiest/golden-earring.text:
Golden Earring was founded in 1961 in The Hague by the guitarist George Kooymans and the bassist Rinus Gerritsen. The group was originally called The Golden Earrings and dropped the s in 1969. Golden Earring lasted sixty years and is one of the few Dutch rock bands to reach the American charts.

The band began in The Hague's beat scene. In 1965 Please Go was their first hit, and in 1968 Dong-dong-di-ki-di-gi-dong became their first number one in the Netherlands. The singer Barry Hay joined the group in 1967, the drummer Cesar Zuiderwijk in 1970. After that Golden Earring grew into a hard rock band. In 1973 came Radar Love, written by Kooymans and Hay, from the album Moontan. The song is about a man driving to his lover at night. It was a number one in the Netherlands, reached number 7 in England and, in 1974, number 13 in America. In 1982 came Twilight Zone, from the album Cut. Kooymans wrote it after reading the spy novel The Bourne Identity. Helped by a video clip by Dick Maas that was shown a great deal on MTV, it became the band's only top ten hit in America.

Golden Earring showed that a Dutch band could compete internationally in English, like Focus and Shocking Blue. There are hundreds of cover versions of Radar Love, including by U2 and White Lion. In 2021 the group stopped, because Kooymans had the muscle disease ALS. He died in 2025.
artiest/golden-earring.listen: In Radar Love (1973) bass and drums drive like an engine that never stops. Notice the middle section, where the band drops back to just the rhythm and the drums take over, before the chorus comes back in.

artiest/goldie.text:
Goldie is the stage name of Clifford Joseph Price, an English producer, DJ, graffiti artist and actor, born on 19 September 1965 in Walsall and raised in Wolverhampton. He has Jamaican and Scottish roots. At the age of three he was put up for adoption and grew up in children's homes and foster families. He first became known as a graffiti artist, with work in Birmingham and Wolverhampton that featured in the documentary Bombin'. He moved to the United States for graffiti projects and sold gold teeth in New York and Miami. The nickname comes from Goldielocks, a name from his days as a b-boy.

In the 1990s Goldie became a pioneer of British jungle, drum and bass and breakbeat hardcore. He released singles as Rufige Kru and Metalheads and co-founded the label Metalheadz. Inner City Life (1994) is one of his best-known tracks and appears on the album Timeless (1995). Saturnz Return followed in 1998, Sine Tempus: The Soundtrack in 2008, The Journey Man in 2017 and Alpha Omega in 2025. As an actor he appeared in The World Is Not Enough, Snatch and EastEnders.

His music combines heavy, deep basslines and accelerated breakbeats with long, floating, soulful passages. Goldie brought drum and bass out of the underground to a large audience and showed that the style could also sound ambitious and almost symphonic. As a result he is one of the best-known faces of the British jungle and drum and bass scene.
artiest/goldie.listen: Listen to Inner City Life and notice the floating, soulful vocals above a fast, stuttering breakbeat. Can you hear how the deep bass and the light vocals work against each other and complement each other?

artiest/gong-kebyar-de-sebatu.text:
Gong Kebyar de Sebatu is a Balinese gamelan ensemble from Sebatu, a village on Bali. Gong kebyar is a style of Balinese gamelan, an orchestra of mainly metal percussion instruments such as gongs and metallophones, supplemented by drums and cymbals. The style arose in the early twentieth century and is known for its sudden, fierce changes in tempo and volume. The word kebyar refers to such a sudden outburst. Little information is available about the group from Sebatu itself, so this entry is limited to the tradition.

In a gong kebyar many musicians play at once, often in fast, interlocking patterns. Two players complement each other and together form a single high, sparkling melodic line. A drummer leads the ensemble and signals the transitions. Taruna Djaja (1972, in the old spelling) is a piece from this tradition.

For anyone who listens to pop, gong kebyar is interesting for hearing how a large group together forms a single rhythmic whole without harmonic chords. In the twentieth century the music also became known outside Bali and inspired Western composers and electronic musicians.
artiest/gong-kebyar-de-sebatu.listen: Listen to Taruna Djaja and notice the sudden changes between loud and soft and fast and slow. Try to hear how the high instruments play interlocking patterns.

artiest/gorillaz.text:
Gorillaz is an English virtual band, conceived in 1998 by the musician Damon Albarn and the artist Jamie Hewlett. The band consists of four invented characters: 2-D, Murdoc Niccals, Noodle and Russel Hobbs. The voice of 2-D comes from Albarn. The idea arose when the two were watching MTV, a channel that Hewlett found empty. They wanted to make a virtual band as a comment on the manufactured pop music of the moment, the age of the boy bands.

The first album, Gorillaz, was released in 2001. Albarn recorded it in his Studio 13 in London and in Jamaica, with the help of the hip hop producer Dan the Automator. The single Clint Eastwood brought success, and the album went triple platinum in Britain. In 2005 came Demon Days, a darker concept album about the night and a world in decline. Plastic Beach followed in 2010, Humanz in 2017, The Now Now in 2018 and Cracker Island in 2023, among others.

Albarn moved away from the Britpop sound of his band Blur and mixed trip hop, punk rock, dub, Latin influences, hip hop and electronic music with world music, often with a long list of guest artists. Live, Gorillaz first performed with a hidden band, later with projected animations and, since 2010, with a fully visible band. In this way the group proved that a band can also be a cartoon.
artiest/gorillaz.listen: Listen to Clint Eastwood and notice the alternation between 2-D's singing voice and the rap. Hear how the low bassline and the melodica give the song a distinctive, dreamy atmosphere.

artiest/gothic-voices.text:
Gothic Voices is a British vocal ensemble that sings medieval music. The group was founded in 1980 by the scholar and musician Christopher Page. The repertoire runs from the eleventh to the fifteenth century and includes work by composers such as Guillaume de Machaut, Guillaume Du Fay and Hildegard von Bingen, and other music from the Middle Ages and the early Renaissance. Sometimes the group also sings contemporary pieces with a medieval sound.

The sound comes from Page's research into performance practice. He concluded that the accompanying lines in medieval scores were intended for lower singing voices and not for instruments. He demonstrated this in 1981 in broadcasts on BBC Radio 3. The group recorded twenty-three albums for Hyperion, Avie and Linn, three of which won a Gramophone Award.

The first album was A Feather on the Breath of God, with hymns and sequences by Hildegard von Bingen, which became one of Hyperion's biggest commercial successes. It was followed by, among others, The Mirror of Narcissus with songs by Machaut, The Garden of Zephirus, The Service of Venus and Mars and Music for the Lion-Hearted King. With these records a broad public got to hear medieval music, in a clear, pure style without instruments.
artiest/gothic-voices.listen: Listen to A Feather on the Breath of God by Hildegard von Bingen, performed by Gothic Voices, and notice the soft, sustained singing voice. Hear how a long melodic line stands on its own without accompaniment.

artiest/gottfried-huppertz.text:
Gottfried Huppertz was a German composer, born on 11 March 1887 and died on 7 February 1937. He is best known for his music for German Expressionist silent films, such as the science fiction film Metropolis (1927). He studied at the Cologne conservatory and worked in Coburg during the First World War, where in 1910 he made his debut as a singer and actor. In 1920 he went to Berlin as an opera singer at the Nollendorfplatz Theatre.

He dedicated his first composition, Rankende Rosen, to the actor Rudolf Klein-Rogge, who in the early 1920s introduced him to the director Fritz Lang and to Thea von Harbou. He wrote his first film music for Lang's Die Nibelungen (1924). While working on the music for Zur Chronik von Grieshuus, in 1925, he began the score for Metropolis, which became his best-known work. He also wrote songs, but only part of his music has been recorded. He died suddenly of a heart attack in 1937.

Huppertz wrote orchestral music for silent films, which was played by a live orchestra during the screening. The piece Maschinen from Metropolis belongs to the work in which he set the sound of a factory and the menace of the machines to music. In this he is an early forerunner of the film composers who later bound image and sound so closely together that the music itself carries the story.
artiest/gottfried-huppertz.listen: Listen to Maschinen and notice the repetitive, stamping rhythm in the orchestra that evokes the sound of machines. Can you hear how the piece grows ever more menacing and fuller?

artiest/grace-jones.text:
Grace Jones was born in 1948 in Spanish Town, Jamaica. Her parents worked in America, and Grace grew up with her grandmother and a strict step-grandfather, in a strict Pentecostal faith. At thirteen she came to Syracuse, in New York State. She studied theatre, rebelled against her parents' faith and became a model. In 1970 she moved to Paris, where she worked for fashion houses such as Yves Saint Laurent and Kenzo and appeared on the covers of magazines such as Elle.

In 1977 she signed with Island Records. Her first albums, Portfolio, Fame and Muse, were disco, and she belonged to the scene around Studio 54 in New York. From Warm Leatherette (1980) she took a different path. With the rhythm duo Sly & Robbie she made music at the Compass Point studio in the Bahamas in which new wave, reggae, funk and pop come together. Nightclubbing (1981) became her greatest success, with Pull Up to the Bumper and I've Seen That Face Before (Libertango). In 1985 the producer Trevor Horn made Slave to the Rhythm with her. She also acted in films, such as the Bond film A View to a Kill.

Grace Jones stood out for her androgynous, cool appearance, with the angular haircut that she developed together with the designer Jean-Paul Goude. In her case music, fashion and image formed a single whole. In this way she became a model for many artists in music and fashion, and an early face in the discussion about gender. Later she worked with Gorillaz and Beyoncé.
artiest/grace-jones.listen: Listen to Slave to the Rhythm and notice how Trevor Horn builds the song from layers of rhythm, voices and electronic sounds. Hear how Grace Jones's voice becomes one of those layers.

artiest/grace-slick.text:
Grace Slick was actually called Grace Wing and was born in 1939 in Illinois. Her father was a banker, her mother had once sung. The family moved to California, where Grace grew up in Palo Alto. She studied art in New York and Miami and then worked as a model for several years. In 1965 she saw a performance in San Francisco by the newly founded band Jefferson Airplane. She then started a band of her own, The Great Society, with her husband Jerry Slick and his brother Darby. Shortly afterwards she wrote the song White Rabbit, by her own account in an hour.

At the end of 1966 Jefferson Airplane asked her to be their new singer. With her on board the band took on a more psychedelic sound. The album Surrealistic Pillow (1967) featured new recordings of White Rabbit and of Somebody to Love, written by Darby Slick. Both songs became big hits. Jefferson Airplane became one of America's most popular bands, and Slick one of the best-known women in rock. She later sang in Jefferson Starship and Starship, with whom she had number one hits in the 1980s with We Built This City and Nothing's Gonna Stop Us Now.

Slick was a figurehead of the psychedelic scene in San Francisco. In White Rabbit she uses the story of Alice in Wonderland to sing about the effects of mind-expanding drugs. In 1990 she gave up music; rock, she felt, was for young people. After that she turned to painting.
artiest/grace-slick.listen: Listen to White Rabbit by Jefferson Airplane and notice how it is built. Hear how the song begins softly, like a kind of march, and grows steadily louder and fuller, until Grace Slick's voice bursts out at the end.

artiest/graciela.text:
Graciela, in full Felipa Graciela Pérez y Gutiérrez, was a Cuban singer of Cuban music and Latin jazz. She was born on 23 August 1915 in Havana and grew up in the Afro-Cuban district of Jesús María. In the 1930s and 1940s she was for ten years the lead singer of Orquesta Anacaona, an all-women orchestra, before leaving Cuba for the United States. She performed all over the world, together with her adopted older brother Frank Grillo, known as Machito.

In 1943 she was brought to New York by Mario Bauzá, when Machito had to join the army. She became the orchestra's lead singer until Machito returned in 1944, and from that moment the three stood on stage together until their split in 1975. Over thirty-two years they travelled through the United States and the rest of the world and, from 1946, played at the Palladium Ballroom. Her best-known recordings are Esta es Graciela, Íntimo y Sentimental and Esa Soy Yo, Yo Soy Así. The album Afro-Cuban Jazz also appeared in 1985.

In 2006 she received the Chico O'Farrill Lifetime Achievement Award from Latin Jazz USA. She died in 2010 in New York, aged 94, and was regarded as the first lady of Latin jazz. With Machito and Bauzá she helped bring Cuban rhythms and jazz together.
artiest/graciela.listen: Listen to a recording of Graciela with Machito's orchestra and notice how the percussionists play a Cuban rhythm while the horns answer in a jazz-like way. Hear how her voice rises above it all.

artiest/graham-coxon.text:
Graham Coxon was born in 1969 in Rinteln, in West Germany, where his father served in the British Army as a clarinettist and bandleader. He grew up in Colchester, in England. There, at the age of eleven, he got to know Damon Albarn at school. At first Coxon played saxophone on Albarn's songs, later guitar in small bands in Colchester. He studied fine art at Goldsmiths College in London, where he met the bassist Alex James. His great musical example was Syd Barrett of Pink Floyd.

His band Seymour changed its name to Blur at the insistence of the record company. Coxon played all the guitars, sang backing vocals and sometimes drummed. At the time of the Britpop battle with Oasis in 1995 he became increasingly distrustful of the music industry. His fondness for lo-fi and alternative music pulled Blur towards a less commercial sound in the late 1990s. He sang the lead vocal on Coffee & TV himself. In 2002 he left the band, after treatment for his alcohol addiction. In 2009 Blur got back together, and new albums such as The Magic Whip followed later.

Since 1998 Coxon has made solo records, on which he plays all the instruments himself. Happiness in Magazines (2004) became his greatest success. He also designs the sleeves of his records, and that of Blur's album 13. His guitar playing is restless, with sliding chords, short runs and broken chords, according to one critic more influenced by his saxophone lessons than by ordinary guitar lessons. Noel Gallagher of Oasis called him one of the most talented guitarists of his generation.
artiest/graham-coxon.listen: Listen to Coffee & TV by Blur, on which Graham Coxon sings himself. Notice his restrained way of singing, very different from Damon Albarn's, and his idiosyncratic guitar parts.

artiest/graham-johnson.text:
Graham Johnson is a British pianist, best known as an accompanist of Lieder. He was born on 10 July 1950 in Bulawayo in Rhodesia, the son of a father who played piano and saxophone. In 1967 he went to the Royal Academy of Music, and later he studied with Gerald Moore and Geoffrey Parsons. A recital by Peter Pears and Benjamin Britten in 1972 led him to choose to become a song accompanist.

In 1976 he founded The Songmakers' Almanac, together with singers such as Felicity Lott, Ann Murray, Anthony Rolfe Johnson and Richard Jackson, to bring forgotten song repertoire to attention. His great project for the Hyperion label was a series of thirty-seven CDs containing all the songs of Franz Schubert. Series of songs by Schumann and by French composers such as Fauré followed. His first recording for Hyperion was Voices of the Night (1980). He is also known for his extensive liner notes, and has written books, including The French Song Companion.

Johnson received an OBE, several Gramophone Awards and, in 2018, the Schubert Prize of the German Schubert Gesellschaft, among other honours. He is professor of accompaniment at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama. His work shows that in song the pianist is an equal partner of the singer.
artiest/graham-johnson.listen: Listen to a song by Schubert from the Hyperion Schubert Edition and notice how the piano does not merely accompany but itself depicts the water, the wind or the unrest. Hear how singer and pianist breathe together.

artiest/graham-nash.text:
Graham Nash was born in 1942 in Blackpool and grew up in Salford, near Manchester. As early as 1955 he sang in a duo with his schoolfriend Allan Clarke. In the early 1960s the two founded The Hollies, one of the most successful English pop groups. The group became known for three-part harmony singing and simple pop songs, influenced by Buddy Holly and The Everly Brothers. Nash often sang the middle sections and was lead singer on On a Carousel and Carrie Anne (1967), among others. He encouraged the group to write songs of their own.

On a tour of America he got to know David Crosby of The Byrds and Stephen Stills of Buffalo Springfield. In 1968 he left The Hollies and formed Crosby, Stills & Nash with them. Their debut album brought a Grammy for Best New Artist. In 1969 Neil Young joined. Nash wrote many of the group's biggest hits, such as Marrakesh Express and Teach Your Children, which The Hollies had earlier turned down, and Our House, about the house in Laurel Canyon that he shared with Joni Mitchell. Later he worked a great deal as a duo with Crosby.

Nash has a light tenor voice. His songs are mostly simple and melodic. In California he became politically active, with songs against the Vietnam War such as Military Madness and Chicago, and later with campaigns against nuclear power. Within the often quarrelling group he was known as the diplomat who held everything together. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame twice.
artiest/graham-nash.listen: Listen to Our House by Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young and notice the harmony singing. Hear how the voices lie close together and form a single sound, with Nash's light voice as lead singer.

artiest/gram-parsons.text:
Gram Parsons was actually called Ingram Cecil Connor and was born in 1946 in Winter Haven, Florida, into a wealthy family of fruit growers. His youth was unhappy: his father committed suicide, and on the day Gram finished high school his mother died. He took his stepfather's surname. After an Elvis Presley concert in 1956 he wanted to make music. He first played rock 'n' roll and then folk, and briefly studied at Harvard. Thanks to a family trust fund he always had money enough.

In 1966 he started the International Submarine Band with musicians from Boston, which later moved to Los Angeles. In 1968 he joined The Byrds. He persuaded the band to record the country album Sweetheart of the Rodeo in Nashville, including his own song Hickory Wind. He left that same year. With The Flying Burrito Brothers he made The Gilded Palace of Sin, which sold little but was praised by critics. He sang his solo records GP (1973) and Grievous Angel (1974) together with the young Emmylou Harris. Parsons died in 1973, aged 26, from a combination of alcohol and morphine.

Parsons called his music Cosmic American Music: a mixture of country, soul, rhythm and blues, folk and rock. He is regarded as a founding father of country rock and alternative country. His body of work is small, but his influence is great. Mick Jagger and Keith Richards of The Rolling Stones learned to appreciate country music through him.
artiest/gram-parsons.listen: Listen to Hickory Wind by The Byrds, sung by Gram Parsons. Notice how a rock band sounds like a country band here, and how Parsons sings in a soft, wistful voice about homesickness for the South.

artiest/grand-mixer-d-st.text:
Grand Mixer D.ST, later known as GrandMixer DXT, is the stage name of Derek Showard, an American musician and DJ. His first name refers to Delancey Street on the Lower East Side of Manhattan in New York. He is regarded as a pioneer of hip hop, and as the first turntablist: the first to make the turntable sound like a fully fledged, improvising musical instrument.

He devised the technique of changing the pitch of a note or sound on the record. In the early years of hip hop a DJ was someone who played records and mixed them together. With his work he showed that you can also play a melody or a solo with two turntables. He appeared in the influential hip hop film Wild Style.

His best-known contribution is the scratching on Rockit, the single by Herbie Hancock from the album Future Shock, which Bill Laswell and Material produced. That track brought scratching to a large audience and helped make the DJ's craft popular. Later he also appeared in the 2001 documentary Scratch. His work shows that the turntable can be an instrument.
artiest/grand-mixer-d-st.listen: Listen to Rockit by Herbie Hancock and notice the scratch sounds that run through the song as a kind of percussion and as a solo. Hear how the turntable plays along there as an instrument.

artiest/grand-wizzard-theodore.text:
Grand Wizzard Theodore is really called Theodore Livingston and was born in 1963 in the Bronx, in New York. In that borough hip hop arose in the 1970s, at parties where DJs played records for dancers. His older brother Mean Gene was a DJ and taught him from an early age how to work with turntables.

In 1975 Theodore was playing records in his bedroom with the volume turned right up. His mother came in angrily and told him to turn the music down. While she stood in the doorway, he held the record with his hand and unconsciously rubbed it back and forth under the needle. That produced a scratching sound. When his mother had gone, he realised that he liked that sound. He practised with it and played the new technique at a party: scratching was born. He also became known for his needle drop, in which he lowered the needle onto exactly the right spot on a record.

In the early 1980s he was part of Grandwizard Theodore & the Fantastic Five, who released Can I Get a Soul Clap in 1982. He also appeared in the hip hop film Wild Style (1983) and worked on the soundtrack. Scratching changed the turntable from a playback device into a musical instrument, and became a fixed part of hip hop. His shout Say turn it up from Fantastic Freaks at the Dixie was later sampled by Public Enemy, among others, in Bring the Noise.
artiest/grand-wizzard-theodore.listen: Listen to a scratch in a hip hop track from the 1980s, for instance Bring the Noise by Public Enemy. Notice the scratching sound that arises when the DJ moves a record back and forth by hand, and how that sound works as a rhythm instrument.

artiest/grandmaster-flash.text:
Grandmaster Flash is the stage name of Joseph Saddler, born on 1 January 1958 in New York and raised in the Bronx. There, in the 1970s, he played at parties in parks and community centres, in the world in which hip hop arose. He was less interested in whole songs than in the drum breaks: the short passages in which only the rhythm carries on and which sent the dancers wild.

To make those breaks longer he developed what he himself called the Quick Mix Theory. He placed two copies of the same record on two turntables and switched between them, so that the break began again and again. In doing so he perfected techniques such as the backspin and punch phrasing, and he helped make scratching popular. On The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash on the Wheels of Steel (1981) you can hear how he builds a new track from pieces of other records. It is regarded as the first record on which scratching was captured.

With his group, Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five, which included the rappers Melle Mel and Kidd Creole, he released The Message in 1982 on the Sugar Hill label. That song made rap more than party music: it describes poverty, violence and hopelessness in the city. In 2002 it was added to the archive of the Library of Congress. In 2007 the group became the first hip hop group inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, and in 2019 Flash became the first hip hop artist to receive the Polar Music Prize.
artiest/grandmaster-flash.listen: In The Message, listen to the slow tempo and the synthesizer line that keeps returning, and to how bare the accompaniment stays so that every line of the lyrics can be understood. Also notice the ending, in which the music stops and a scene on the street can be heard.

artiest/grandmaster-flash-en-the-furious.text:
Grandmaster Flash & The Furious Five was formed in 1978 in the South Bronx in New York. DJ Grandmaster Flash worked with five MCs: Melle Mel, Kidd Creole, Keef Cowboy, Scorpio and Rahiem. Flash developed techniques for switching between two records faster and more precisely. The group is important because with The Message it showed that rap could be more than party music: a report on life in the city.

Around 1980 the group signed with Sylvia Robinson's Sugar Hill Records. The first single there, Freedom (1980), reached number 19 on the R&B chart. In 1981 Flash made The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash on the Wheels of Steel, a record that he mixed live on several turntables, with scratching in it. The Message (1982) was written by Duke Bootee, Melle Mel, Jiggs Chase and Sylvia Robinson. The tempo is slow, the space in the arrangement is large. Melle Mel raps about poverty, noise, crime and a boy who ends up in prison. Grandmaster Flash himself does not play on it. In England The Message reached number 8, in the Dutch Top 40 number 6.

In 1983 a quarrel with Sugar Hill over royalties followed, and the group split into two camps. In 2002 The Message became the first hip hop recording to enter the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry. In 2007 the group became the first hip hop group inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. In 2012 Rolling Stone named The Message the best hip hop song of all time.
artiest/grandmaster-flash-en-the-furious.listen: The Message (1982): notice how slow and bare the beat is compared with Rapper's Delight. A synthesizer line keeps returning, and in that open space every line from Melle Mel stands out.
